What must he do?","fact_ids":["sec13-F04","sec13-F03"]},"answer":{"text":"Yield to the pedestrian in the unmarked crosswalk.","fact_ids":["sec13-F04"]},"rationale":{"text":"Every corner has a crosswalk, and drivers must yield to a pedestrian crossing in an unmarked one, or stop and stay stopped in a marked one.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Pedestrians come first","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Drivers carry the primary duty.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03"]},{"text":"Speed decides survival.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03"]},{"text":"Every corner has a crosswalk.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"This section is about sharing the road with everyone who is not in a car, and it starts with pedestrians. Pedestrian safety is shared, but drivers carry the primary duty to prevent crashes with pedestrians, who are the most vulnerable road users. In this lesson we look at how speed changes a pedestrian's chance of surviving a crash, where crosswalks are even when no lines are painted, what drivers must do at marked and unmarked crosswalks, what happens when the signal changes mid-crossing, the penalties for failing to stop, and what pedestrians themselves must do.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Speed and survival","fact_ids":["sec13-F02","sec13-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Twenty miles per hour: about five percent.","fact_ids":["sec13-F02","sec13-F01"]},{"text":"Forty miles per hour: eighty-five percent.","fact_ids":["sec13-F02","sec13-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"The manual gives two figures that show why speed matters around pedestrians. A pedestrian struck by a car at twenty miles per hour has about a five percent chance of dying. At forty miles per hour, that rate jumps to eighty-five percent. Doubling the speed takes the risk from a small chance to a likely death. That is the background for every rule in this lesson. Because pedestrians are the most vulnerable road users, and because the outcome of a crash depends so heavily on speed, drivers are the ones expected to slow down, look carefully and give way.","fact_ids":["sec13-F02","sec13-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Marked and unmarked crosswalks","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F04","sec13-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Every corner has a crosswalk.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F04","sec13-F05"]},{"text":"Marked: stop and stay stopped.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F04","sec13-F05"]},{"text":"Unmarked: yield.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F04","sec13-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Every corner of an intersection has a crosswalk, even when no lines are painted, and this is called an unmarked crosswalk. Drivers must stop and stay stopped for a pedestrian in a marked crosswalk, and yield to a pedestrian crossing in an unmarked one. So the absence of paint never means the absence of a crosswalk. If the signal changes from WALK to DON'T WALK while a pedestrian is crossing, the driver must still stop. A driver may never block or park in a crosswalk, and may never pass a vehicle that is stopped at one.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F04","sec13-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Paint or no paint","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F05","sec13-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"No lines still means a crosswalk.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F05","sec13-F04"]},{"text":"Signal change: still stop.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F05","sec13-F04"]},{"text":"Never pass a stopped car.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F05","sec13-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Many questions assume that a crosswalk exists only where lines are painted. The manual says every corner of an intersection has a crosswalk, marked or unmarked. A second trap is the signal change. If the signal changes to DON'T WALK while someone is still crossing, you must still stop for that pedestrian. A third is the stopped car. If a vehicle ahead of you is stopped at a crosswalk, you may never pass it, because it may be stopped for a pedestrian. Each of these rules protects a pedestrian who is already on the road.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F05","sec13-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Penalties and multi-lane stops","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-F07","sec13-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Fines, jail, service, points, suspension.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-F07","sec13-F08"]},{"text":"Tougher with serious injury.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-F07","sec13-F08"]},{"text":"Stop well short on multi-lane roads.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-F07","sec13-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Failing to stop for a pedestrian can mean fines, possible jail, community service, points and license suspension, with tougher penalties if serious bodily injury results. On a road with several lanes, stop well short of the crosswalk so you do not hide the pedestrian from drivers in the next lanes. Pedestrians have duties too. They must obey signals and may not step suddenly into the path of a car that is too close to yield. But their mistakes never excuse a driver from using due care. So even when a pedestrian is wrong, the driver is still expected to take care.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-F07","sec13-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the corner","fact_ids":["sec13-F04","sec13-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"No painted lines.","fact_ids":["sec13-F04","sec13-F03"]},{"text":"Pedestrian stepping off.","fact_ids":["sec13-F04","sec13-F03"]},{"text":"Stop, yield or go?","fact_ids":["sec13-F04","sec13-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: Jamal is driving through a neighborhood and reaches a corner with no painted lines. Jamal must yield. Every corner of an intersection has a crosswalk even when no lines are painted, called an unmarked crosswalk, and drivers must yield to a pedestrian crossing in an unmarked one. What should she check first?","fact_ids":["sec13-F10"]},"answer":{"text":"Left, right and behind, her mirrors and blind spots, and the crosswalk for pedestrians.","fact_ids":["sec13-F10"]},"rationale":{"text":"Before any turn, especially a right on red, scan in all directions, check mirrors and blind spots, and look for pedestrians in or entering the crosswalk.","fact_ids":["sec13-F10","sec13-R06"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec13-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Where pedestrians appear","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-R06","sec13-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Schools, stops and parks.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-R06","sec13-R07"]},{"text":"Turns and driveways.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-R06","sec13-R07"]},{"text":"Night and bad weather.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-R06","sec13-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Knowing the rules for crosswalks is only half the job. We finish with pedestrians walking where there are no sidewalks, and why their precautions never reduce your own duty to stay vigilant. The pattern is the same each time: a driver focused on finding a gap in traffic forgets that someone on foot may be crossing the path of the turn. How should she check her blind spot?","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-R11"]},"answer":{"text":"Twice, by turning her head rather than relying on mirrors alone.","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-R11"]},"rationale":{"text":"Riders may react differently, so check blind spots twice before changing lanes or turning, and turn your head rather than relying on mirrors alone.","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-R11"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Seeing motorcycles","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-F15","sec13-R10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Same laws, different reactions.","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-F15","sec13-R10"]},{"text":"Notice them first.","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-F15","sec13-R10"]},{"text":"Leave plenty of room.","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-F15","sec13-R10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Motorcycles share the road under the same laws as cars and trucks, but they are smaller and riders may react differently. In this lesson we cover how to check for motorcycles before changing lanes, why you should never follow one too closely, what to do when one passes you, the most common cause of motorcycle crashes, the pavement hazards that make riders swerve, and where to watch hardest. The thread running through all of it is noticing: most of what goes wrong between cars and motorcycles starts with a driver who never saw the motorcycle at all.","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-F15","sec13-R10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Checking for motorcycles","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-R11","sec13-R10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Same laws apply.","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-R11","sec13-R10"]},{"text":"Check blind spots twice.","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-R11","sec13-R10"]},{"text":"Turn your head, not just mirrors.","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-R11","sec13-R10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Laws for cars and trucks also apply to motorcycles, but a rider may react differently, so check blind spots twice before changing lanes or turning. Before turning, parallel parking, opening a door or pulling from the curb, check blind spots by turning your head rather than relying on mirrors alone. Watch for motorcycles at intersections and when turning left, always signal, and leave plenty of room between your car and a motorcycle. So the motorcycle habits are simple but specific: signal, look twice, turn your head, and keep space between you and the rider.","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-R11","sec13-R10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Following and being passed","fact_ids":["sec13-F13","sec13-F14"]},"lines":[{"text":"Never follow too closely.","fact_ids":["sec13-F13","sec13-F14"]},{"text":"Motorcycles may stop shorter.","fact_ids":["sec13-F13","sec13-F14"]},{"text":"Being passed: hold speed and position.","fact_ids":["sec13-F13","sec13-F14"]}],"narration":{"text":"Never follow a motorcycle too closely, because it may be able to stop in a shorter distance than other vehicles. If the rider stops quickly, a car following too closely may not be able to stop in time. When a motorcycle passes you, keep your speed and position and give it room to finish the pass. Do not speed up or drift toward it. These two rules are mirror images: behind a motorcycle you give it room in front of you, and when it passes you, you give it room beside and in front of you. In both cases, extra space protects the rider.","fact_ids":["sec13-F13","sec13-F14"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Why riders swerve","fact_ids":["sec13-R09","sec13-R10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Slippery or uneven pavement.","fact_ids":["sec13-R09","sec13-R10"]},{"text":"Grooves and gratings.","fact_ids":["sec13-R09","sec13-R10"]},{"text":"Expect a sudden swerve.","fact_ids":["sec13-R09","sec13-R10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap about rider behavior. A motorcycle that swerves suddenly can look careless, but the manual explains why it happens. Slippery, sloped or uneven pavement and grooves or gratings are hazards for motorcycle riders, so anticipate a rider swerving around something a car would ignore. Something a car would roll over without a second thought can be a hazard to a rider. So when you share a lane area with a motorcycle, leave enough room for it to move around these hazards, and do not assume the rider will hold a perfectly straight line.","fact_ids":["sec13-R09","sec13-R10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The most common crash cause","fact_ids":["sec13-F15","sec13-R10","sec13-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Drivers fail to notice motorcycles.","fact_ids":["sec13-F15","sec13-R10","sec13-F12"]},{"text":"Watch intersections and left turns.","fact_ids":["sec13-F15","sec13-R10","sec13-F12"]},{"text":"Always signal.","fact_ids":["sec13-F15","sec13-R10","sec13-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"The most common cause of motorcycle crashes is a driver failing to notice and recognize the motorcycle in traffic. That is why so many of the rules in this lesson are about looking: checking blind spots twice, turning your head instead of relying on mirrors, and watching for motorcycles at intersections and when turning left. Always signal, so a rider knows what you plan to do, and leave plenty of room between your car and a motorcycle. If you build these checks into every lane change and turn, you directly address the leading cause of motorcycle crashes.","fact_ids":["sec13-F15","sec13-R10","sec13-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the lane change","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-R11","sec13-F15"]},"lines":[{"text":"Motorcycle nearby.","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-R11","sec13-F15"]},{"text":"Changing lanes.","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-R11","sec13-F15"]},{"text":"How do you check?","fact_ids":["sec13-F12","sec13-R11","sec13-F15"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: Lena is on a busy road and wants to move into the next lane.
